chapters.n: James, a leader of the early Church in Jerusalem and the Lord’s brother, writes to believing Jews scattered across the Roman world. He calls himself simply a servant, not boasting of his family tie to Jesus.

f.g: Traditionally James the brother of the Lord, not James the son of Zebedee.
Greek diaspora — Israelites living outside the Holy Land.

chapters.n: James opens with a surprising command: treat hard trials as a reason for joy. He does not mean trials feel good, but that God can use them for our growth.

f.g: divers = various; temptations here means trials of every kind. The JST reads ‘many afflictions.’

chapters.n: The reason for joy: when faith is tested, it produces endurance. Like a muscle under strain, faith grows stronger by being tried.

f.g: Greek hypomonē — steady endurance, staying power under pressure.

chapters.n: Let endurance finish its work. The goal is to become whole and mature—complete in character, not lacking anything God wants us to become.

f.g: Greek teleios — complete, mature, fully developed.
wanting = lacking.

chapters.n: This is the verse that sent fourteen-year-old Joseph Smith into the woods to pray in 1820. James promises that God gives wisdom generously to anyone who asks and never scolds them for asking.

f.g: upbraid = scold or reproach; God does not shame us for asking.

chapters.n: The asking must come with real trust. A person who keeps flip-flopping is like ocean surf pushed back and forth by the wind—never settled in one direction.

f.g: Not doubting; not divided between trust and distrust.

chapters.n: Someone who prays while privately expecting nothing should not be surprised to receive nothing. Faith is the channel through which God’s answers come.
A “double minded” person has two souls pulling in opposite directions. Divided loyalty makes a person unsteady in every part of life, not just in prayer.

f.g: Greek dipsychos — literally ‘two-souled.’

chapters.n: James turns to rich and poor. The poor believer can rejoice because, in Christ, he is lifted up and made an heir of God’s kingdom.

f.g: Humble or poor in worldly standing.

chapters.n: The rich believer should rejoice in being humbled, because wealth is as short-lived as a wildflower. Recognizing that keeps him honest about what really lasts.
James paints a scene from Palestine: the hot sun and dry east wind can wither the fields in a day. Wealth fades just as fast, even while the rich man is busy with his plans.

f.g: Possibly the scorching east wind (sirocco) that withers vegetation.
The beauty of its appearance.

chapters.n: The one who endures testing faithfully is truly happy. Like a victorious athlete, he will receive a crown—here, eternal life—promised to those who love God.
Don’t blame God for temptations to do evil. God is untouched by evil and never lures anyone into sin.

f.g: God allows us to be tested, but He never entices anyone toward sin.

chapters.n: Temptation comes from inside us—our own desires drag us away and bait the hook. James uses fishing and hunting images for being lured.

f.g: Strong desire of any kind, not only sexual desire.
Literally ‘baited,’ like luring a fish.

chapters.n: James traces sin’s life cycle like a birth: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin, fully grown, gives birth to death. Stopping temptation early stops the whole chain.
A short, loving warning: don’t be deceived about where evil and good come from.
Everything truly good comes from God, the Creator of the heavenly lights. Unlike the sun and moon, which shift and cast moving shadows, God never changes.

f.g: God as creator of the sun, moon and stars.

chapters.n: God chose to give us new spiritual birth through the gospel message. We are like the first and best of the harvest, offered to Him.

f.g: The first part of a harvest, dedicated to God under the law of Moses.

chapters.n: James gives timeless counsel: listen quickly, speak slowly, and be slow to anger. It is simple advice for families, friendships, and online life alike.
Human anger doesn’t produce the kind of right living God wants. Getting angry rarely makes anything holier.
So strip off moral filth and the overflow of wickedness, and humbly welcome God’s word, which can take root inside you and save you.

f.g: An overflow or excess of wickedness; naughtiness = evil.
The word ‘implanted’ or rooted in you, like a seed.

chapters.n: Hearing the gospel is not enough; we must act on it. Those who only listen are fooling themselves about where they stand.
James compares a listener who doesn’t act to someone glancing in a mirror. Ancient mirrors were polished metal and gave only a dim reflection.

f.g: A mirror, usually polished bronze in that day.

chapters.n: He looks, walks away, and immediately forgets what he saw. Gospel truth shows us who we really are, but it only helps if we remember and change.
By contrast, someone who looks closely into God’s law and keeps living it will be blessed in what he does. God’s law is called the law of liberty because it frees us.
Outward religion means little if a person can’t control his speech. An unbridled tongue shows that someone is fooling himself about his devotion.

f.g: Like a horse without a bridle—uncontrolled.
Empty, worthless.

chapters.n: James defines true religion in practical terms: care for orphans and widows in their struggles, and stay morally clean in a corrupt world.
James warns that faith in the glorious Lord Jesus cannot go together with favoritism. Treating people differently based on status contradicts the Savior we follow.

f.g: Favoritism; judging people by outward rank or wealth.

chapters.n: He imagines a scene at church: a wealthy man walks in wearing gold rings and fine clothes, and a poor man arrives in dirty, shabby clothing.

f.g: Greek synagōgē — the gathering place or meeting of believers.
Filthy, ragged clothing.

chapters.n: If the members rush to give the rich man the best seat while telling the poor man to stand or sit on the floor, something has gone badly wrong.

f.g: gay = bright, splendid, showy.
On the floor by my feet—a place of humiliation.

chapters.n: Such favoritism makes us biased judges with wrong motives, ranking people by appearance instead of seeing them as God does.

f.g: Judges whose reasoning is corrupt.

chapters.n: God has often chosen people the world calls poor to be rich in faith and heirs of His kingdom. The Lord’s values turn worldly rankings upside down.
James points out the irony: the members insulted the poor, yet it was the wealthy who were exploiting them and dragging them into court.

f.g: Courts of law, where creditors could press poor debtors.

chapters.n: These same powerful people mock the holy name of Christ by which believers are called. Why honor those who dishonor the Lord?

f.g: The name of Christ, taken upon believers.

chapters.n: The “royal law”—the King’s own law—is to love your neighbor as yourself. Living by it is exactly what God wants.

f.g: The supreme law, given by the King.

chapters.n: Playing favorites is not a minor social mistake; it is sin, and the law itself exposes it as breaking God’s commandment.

f.g: convinced = convicted, shown to be guilty.

chapters.n: God’s law is a unified whole. Breaking even one part still makes a person a lawbreaker—which is why everyone needs Christ’s mercy.
The same God gave all the commandments. Avoiding one sin while committing another still leaves a person guilty before Him.
Speak and act like people who know they will be judged by the law that frees us—the gospel of Christ.
The merciless will face judgment without mercy, but mercy wins out over judgment. Showing mercy invites God’s mercy toward us.
James begins his famous teaching: what good is claiming faith if it never shows in action? That kind of “faith” cannot save.

f.g: Literally ‘can that faith save him?’—meaning a faith with no works.

chapters.n: He gives an example: a fellow believer has no clothes and nothing to eat that day.

f.g: Often meant poorly or insufficiently clothed.

chapters.n: If someone just says “Go in peace, stay warm and well fed” and gives nothing, those kind words are useless. Real compassion acts.
Faith that produces no works is like a corpse—lifeless. True faith naturally shows itself in deeds.
James imagines a debate. Someone claims faith and works are separate gifts; James answers that you can’t show faith except through what you do.

f.g: shew = show.

chapters.n: Believing that God is one is good—but even demons believe that, and it only makes them shudder. Knowing facts about God is not the same as faith.

f.g: An echo of the Shema, Israel’s core confession.

chapters.n: James calls the objector an “empty” person and asks if he is willing to learn that faith without works is useless.

f.g: Empty or foolish person.

chapters.n: Abraham’s faith was proven when he obeyed God and offered Isaac on the altar. His belief showed itself in a costly act.
Abraham’s faith and his actions worked together, and his obedience brought his faith to full maturity.

f.g: Completed, brought to its goal.

chapters.n: His obedience fulfilled the scripture that Abraham believed God and was counted righteous. He even became known as the Friend of God.
James concludes that people are justified by faith that works, not by bare belief. Paul and James agree: real faith shows itself in obedience.
Rahab, a Canaanite woman in Jericho, also showed faith by action when she hid Israel’s spies and helped them escape.
James sums it up with a vivid image: a body without its spirit is dead, and so is faith without works.
Not many should rush to become teachers, James warns, because those who teach others are held to a stricter standard.

f.g: Greek didaskaloi — teachers.

chapters.n: Everyone stumbles in many ways. Someone who never slips in speech would be a mature, complete person, able to control the rest of himself too.

f.g: Stumble, make a mistake.
Mature, complete—not flawless in every sense.

chapters.n: A small bit in a horse’s mouth steers the whole powerful animal. In the same way, controlling the tongue helps steer one’s whole life.

f.g: The metal mouthpiece of a bridle.

chapters.n: Huge ships pushed by strong winds are still turned by a small rudder wherever the pilot chooses. Small things can direct great ones.

f.g: Rudder.
The pilot wishes; list = to choose or desire.

chapters.n: The tongue is small but makes big claims and has big effects. One spark can set a whole forest ablaze.

f.g: How great a forest or woodland.

chapters.n: James uses strong images: careless or hateful speech is like fire fed by hell itself. It can corrupt a person and set the whole course of life burning.

f.g: Literally ‘the wheel of birth’—the whole cycle of human life.
Greek Gehenna, the burning valley outside Jerusalem used as an image of punishment.

chapters.n: Humans have tamed animals of every kind—wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and sea creatures.
Yet no one can fully tame the tongue by himself. It is restless and can spread poison like a snake. We need God’s help to govern our words.
We use the same tongue to praise God and to curse people—people made in God’s own image. That contradiction is the problem.

f.g: Likeness or image of God.

chapters.n: Blessing and cursing flowing from the same mouth should not be. Our speech should be consistent with our worship.
James uses nature to make his point: a spring doesn’t pour out sweet and bitter water from the same opening.

f.g: A spring of water.

chapters.n: A fig tree can’t grow olives, and a grapevine can’t grow figs. What comes out of us reveals what we really are inside.
Who is truly wise? Let him show it by a good way of life and by actions done with the humility that wisdom brings.

f.g: In KJV English, conduct or way of life, not just talking.

chapters.n: If your heart is full of bitter jealousy and selfish ambition, don’t brag about being wise—that would be a lie against the truth.

f.g: Selfish ambition or rivalry.

chapters.n: That kind of “wisdom” doesn’t come from heaven. It is worldly, driven by natural appetites, and even demonic in origin.

f.g: Natural or unspiritual—governed by the physical self.

chapters.n: Where jealousy and rivalry rule, disorder and every kind of evil follow. Envy breaks families, wards, and communities apart.

f.g: Disorder, instability.

chapters.n: Heavenly wisdom is described in a list worth memorizing: pure, peace-loving, gentle, open to reason, merciful, fruitful, fair, and sincere.

f.g: Willing to listen and be persuaded.

chapters.n: Peacemakers plant seeds in peace and harvest righteousness. Good outcomes grow out of a peaceful spirit.
Where do quarrels and fights among you come from? James answers: from selfish desires battling inside each person. Outer conflict starts with inner conflict.

f.g: Cravings for pleasure or possessions.
The parts of the body—the whole self.

chapters.n: People crave things, grow jealous, even become violent, and still end up empty. Often they never simply ask God for what they truly need.
Sometimes prayers go unanswered because they are selfish—asking only to feed our own cravings. God answers prayers that align with His will.

f.g: Ask wrongly, with bad motives.

chapters.n: Using Old Testament language, James calls worldly believers “adulterers,” unfaithful to God like a spouse who cheats. Loving the world’s values puts us at odds with God.

f.g: A prophetic image of spiritual unfaithfulness to God, Israel’s ‘husband.’
Hostility.

chapters.n: A hard verse to translate. James seems to say God jealously longs for the spirit He placed in us—He wants our undivided love. No exact Old Testament quote matches.

f.g: Possibly ‘yearns jealously’—God’s jealous love for His people.

chapters.n: But God gives even more grace to meet our weakness. He opposes the proud but helps the humble.
So yield yourselves to God and stand firm against the devil. When resisted, Satan’s power to tempt us retreats.
A beautiful promise: come near to God and He will come near to you. Clean your actions and purify your motives, you who are torn between God and the world.
James calls for real sorrow for sin rather than careless laughter. This godly sorrow is the first step of repentance, not a call to be gloomy forever.

f.g: Dejection, sorrow.

chapters.n: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will raise you up. God lifts those who stop trying to lift themselves.
Don’t slander one another. Condemning a fellow believer puts you above God’s law of love, acting as its judge instead of obeying it.
Only God, the one Lawgiver, can save or destroy. Who are we to condemn our neighbor?
James turns to confident business travelers who plan a year of profit as if their future were guaranteed.

f.g: An old phrase meaning ‘Come now!’ or ‘Listen!’

chapters.n: You don’t know what tomorrow holds. Life is like a puff of steam or morning mist—here a moment, then gone.
Instead, plan with humility: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Planning is fine; forgetting God is not.
Bragging about your own plans as if you controlled the future is wrong. Arrogant boasting leaves God out.

f.g: Arrogant pretensions or bragging.

chapters.n: A key principle: knowing the right thing to do and not doing it is sin. Sins of omission matter as much as sins of commission.
James speaks like an Old Testament prophet to rich oppressors: weep and wail, for misery is coming. The warning targets those who gained wealth by injustice.
Their hoarded wealth is already rotting and their fine clothes are eaten by moths. Earthly treasure does not last.
Their gold and silver are corroded, and that corrosion will testify against them. They piled up riches even as the last days were drawing near.

f.g: Corroded, rusted (gold doesn’t literally rust—James is making a moral point).

chapters.n: The wages they cheated from their harvest workers cry out, and God—the Lord of armies—has heard those cries.

f.g: Hebrew ‘Lord of hosts’—Lord of armies.

chapters.n: They lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattening themselves like cattle—unaware that it was a day of slaughter for them.

f.g: Self-indulgent, unrestrained.

chapters.n: They condemned and killed innocent people who did not fight back. Many readers also see here the Righteous One, Jesus, who submitted without resistance.

f.g: The righteous one.

chapters.n: To the oppressed believers James says: be patient until the Lord comes. A farmer waits for the autumn and spring rains before the harvest.

f.g: In Palestine the early rain falls in autumn after sowing; the latter rain in spring before harvest.
Farmer.

chapters.n: So be patient and strengthen your hearts; the Lord’s coming is near.

f.g: Establish, make firm.

chapters.n: Don’t grumble against each other in hard times. The Judge is already standing at the door, ready to enter.

f.g: Don’t complain or groan against.

chapters.n: Look to the prophets as models of patiently suffering hardship while faithfully speaking for the Lord.
We call people blessed who endure. Job’s steadfastness shows how the Lord in the end proved full of compassion and mercy.

f.g: Full of pity, compassionate.

chapters.n: Echoing Jesus, James says not to swear oaths to back up what you say. Be so honest that a simple yes or no is enough.
In every situation, turn to God: pray in trouble, sing praises in happy times.
Anyone sick should call the Church elders to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the Lord’s name. Latter-day Saints still follow this pattern in priesthood blessings of the sick.

f.g: Olive oil, consecrated and applied in the Lord’s name.

chapters.n: Prayer offered in faith will help the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. Forgiveness of sins is also offered—healing of body and soul go together.
Admit your faults to one another and pray for each other so you can be healed. The earnest prayer of a righteous person is powerful.

f.g: Working, earnest, energetic.
Accomplishes a great deal.

chapters.n: Elijah was an ordinary human like us, yet his prayer closed the heavens for three and a half years. Ordinary people can pray with extraordinary faith.

f.g: Greek form of the name Elijah.

chapters.n: When Elijah prayed again, rain came and the land produced crops once more.
If a believer wanders from the truth and someone helps bring him back,

f.g: Wander off, stray.

chapters.n: that rescuer saves a soul from spiritual death and helps cover many sins. James ends his letter on the joy of rescuing the lost.
